strengths: The central finding — that directly fine-tuning the value-projection bias (b_v) outperforms fine-tuning b_q or b_k in low-data regimes — is clearly articulated and supported by an unusually broad empirical validation: encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa), decoder-only (OPT-1.3B/6.7B), and bias-free LLMs (LLaMA2-7B, GPT-J-6B, DeepSeek-Coder), across GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, DROP, PAWS-X, and CommonsenseQA, spanning classification, multiple-choice, and generation tasks.

The analytical treatment is simple but plausible: softmax shift-invariance explains why b_k cannot improve expressiveness; the Jacobian/sparsity argument motivates why b_q has limited effect; and the derivation that b_v acts as a direct additive shift on the SDPA output (plus the b_v ≈ b_o equivalence in Appendix B.2) ties the mechanism to the empirical observation.

Statistical rigor is above average for this type of study: paired t-tests for main results, multi-seed mean±std reporting, and documentation of data-regime definitions and full hyperparameter tables in the appendix support reproducibility.

The angular-change metric (Mag+Angle) for ranking bias importance is a reasonable attempt to explain why prior magnitude-based or Fisher-based selection heuristics disagree with downstream performance, and the comparisons against both baselines are informative.
The compatibility experiments (injecting b_v into LoRA/VeRA/DoRA/PiSSA variants) demonstrate that the finding is not merely an artifact of one PEFT setting.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper itself concedes that the concurrent Qiu et al. (2025) gated-attention work already shows that interventions after the value projection are more effective, and that b_v in BEFT 'can be interpreted as a linear variant of the additive gating' from that work. The core deliverable therefore reduces to a simple, largely anticipated recommendation (fine-tune b_v), and the theoretical contribution is an incremental special case.

There is a tension in the paper's central claim of 'no post-hoc evaluation': the final recommendation (always choose b_v) indeed needs no post-hoc step, but then the Mag+Angle metric — the main methodological contribution — is rendered largely redundant, and the metric itself requires fine-tuning all bias terms first to compute changes, which is a post-hoc procedure. The paper does not convincingly establish a use case where the dynamic metric outperforms the fixed rule.

The argument for b_q's limited expressiveness is heuristic: 'the majority of |J_ij| approach zero' does not strictly establish that optimizing b_q has limited expressive capacity (gradient magnitude through the softmax Jacobian is not the same as the achievable effect of changing b_q), so the theory only loosely supports the empirical asymmetry.

Some results suggest degenerate optimization for certain bias terms (e.g., b_k yielding 0.00 F1 on QQP-medium, 6.5 MCC on CoLA), which is acknowledged only implicitly; a discussion of training instability and whether the comparison is fair under shared hyperparameters would strengthen the evidence.

The headline framing overstates the contribution ('unprecedented parameter efficiency'), and comparisons to full fine-tuning/LoRA are confined to particular low-data slices with single hyperparameter settings per cell, leaving open whether tuning budgets would change conclusions.

Writing and presentation issues: heavy repetition of the 'without any post-hoc evaluation' phrase, a convoluted and artifact-laden Figure 3, a missing code URL in the abstract, and citation oddities (a blog post, an 'ICLR 2026' reference) detract from polish.

strengths: The central finding is crisp, actionable, and easy to reproduce: directly fine-tuning the value-projection bias b_v outperforms fine-tuning b_q or b_k in low-data regimes, with negligible parameter cost (0.01-0.04% of parameters).

The empirical validation is unusually broad and thorough: encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa), decoder-only (OPT-1.3B/6.7B), and bias-free LLMs (LLaMA2-7B, GPT-J, DeepSeek-Coder), across GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, DROP, PAWS-X, and CommonsenseQA, plus compatibility with LoRA/VeRA/DoRA/PiSSA.

The paper includes paired t-tests reporting statistical significance for the main comparisons, multi-seed mean±std in the appendix, and detailed hyperparameter tables (Appendix D), which supports reproducibility.

The mechanistic analysis has sound elements: the shift-invariance argument showing b_k cannot improve expressiveness is clean and convincing, and the equivalence derivation between b_v and the output-projection bias b_o (Appendix B.2), supported empirically in Table 7, is a nice observation.
The paper is honest about the concurrent and closely related Qiu et al. (2025) gated-attention work and positions its contribution relative to it.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution reduces to 'fine-tune b_v rather than all biases,' a small delta over BitFit, and the value-projection advantage is anticipated by concurrent gating work (Qiu et al., 2025), which the paper itself acknowledges. The paper reads more as a careful empirical confirmation than a new method.

The angular-change metric (Section 2) is post-hoc and somewhat ad hoc: it requires first fine-tuning all biases and then measuring changes, which costs a full fine-tuning run. The repeated claim of 'without requiring any post-hoc evaluation' is misleading for the selection procedure itself and only holds because b_v wins essentially everywhere - at which point the ranking machinery is unnecessary.

The expressiveness analysis of b_q via the softmax Jacobian is heuristic: the argument that 'the majority of |J_ij| approach zero in high dimensions' conflates small Jacobian entries with limited optimization benefit and lacks formal or ablation support (e.g., temperature scaling or attention-entropy interventions to test the sharpness hypothesis causally).

The importance-ranking metric's usefulness is unclear given its circularity: it is validated by whether the selected bias performs best, but the ranking is computed from a full fine-tuning that already reveals the answer.

Some experimental results are presented without discussion or sanity checks, e.g., b_k collapsing to 0.00 F1 on QQP (Table 1) and 12.9 at high data, and 37.5±0.0 on CB with std 0.0 over three seeds, which suggests degenerate runs that should be explained.

Anomalous/inconsistent reporting details undermine polish: Figure 1's '~30x reduction' annotation is unexplained in the text; Table 2's runtime comparison for a 0.01%-parameter method vs. full fine-tuning on a single small dataset is thin evidence of efficiency claims; the LoRA/VeRA/DoRA 'injected into bias terms' setup (Appendix C.4) is non-standard and under-justified.

Scope limitations are acknowledged but significant: the analysis covers only softmax SDPA attention with q/k/v biases, excluding FFN biases, LayerNorm parameters, and linear attention, so the practical applicability to modern bias-free architectures requires manually adding parameters, which changes the comparison.
Writing and presentation issues: dense paragraph-level claims, some awkward phrasing, and figures (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 4) that are hard to parse without extensive cross-referencing to the appendix.
